task_description: A word problem: in May 2023 someone drives across the U.S. from California to Maine, taking I-40 from Los Angeles to Cincinnati and then I-90 from Cincinnati to Augusta. They drink 5 twelve-ounce water bottles per 100 miles traveled (with mileage rounded to the nearest 100), and recycle the bottles at the trip's end. The task asks how many dollars they get back 'according to Wikipedia.' The gold answer is 8, which implies the correct city-to-city route mileage is far smaller than the full interstate lengths (on the order of ~3,000-3,200 mi rounded → ~3,000-3,200 mi, yielding ~160 bottles at 5 cents = $8), redeemed at Maine's 5 cents/bottle deposit. The team's job was to find the correct leg mileage and the correct deposit rate and multiply.
final_vs_expected: produced $14.25 vs gold 8 — team used the FULL published lengths of I-40 (2,556.61 mi) and I-90 (3,099.74 mi) summed to 5,656 mi instead of the actual LA→Cincinnati and Cincinnati→Augusta city-to-city leg distances, inflating bottle count from ~160 to 285
primary_cause: WebResearcher computed mileage from the full end-to-end lengths of I-40 and I-90 rather than the specified city-to-city legs, and despite the Critic flagging exactly this error, no agent ever obtained or estimated the correct leg distances before finalizing.
mast_rationale: 1.1 (disobey task spec): the task names specific legs ('I-40 from Los Angeles to Cincinnati, then I-90 from Cincinnati to Augusta') but the team substituted the full interstate lengths, ignoring the task's actual distance constraint. 3.3 (incorrect verification / verification theater): the Critic explicitly identified the core defect ('The teammate used the full Wikipedia lengths of I-40 and I-90, which are not the same thing as the mileage for those city-to-city legs') and said 'Stop here until that's addressed,' yet the Finalizer accepted the same unverified $14.25 anyway — the verification request was satisfied in form (WebResearcher re-spoke) but not substance (mileage still unverified). 2.6 (reasoning-action mismatch): WebResearcher's own round-3 reasoning admits 'Cincinnati is on I-75, not I-40' and that the route 'doesn't make sense' / is 'hypothetical,' yet it published the full-length-based $14.25 as the supported number; the Finalizer's reasoning concedes mileage is 'unverified' but it finalizes that very number.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: WebResearcher searches Wikipedia for I-40 and I-90, finding only full-highway lengths (2,556.61 and 3,099.74 mi) plus CRV/Maine deposit pages. Its private reasoning notes Cincinnati is on I-75 not I-40 and that the route may be 'hypothetical,' but it nonetheless sums the two full lengths to 5,656.35 mi → rounds to 5,700 → 285 bottles → publishes refund $14.25 with citations. Turn 2: Critic privately and publicly nails the flaw — the full interstate lengths are not the city-to-city legs, the deposit rule isn't quoted, and redemption jurisdiction (Maine) matters; it explicitly asks WebResearcher to 'verify the actual Wikipedia-supported mileage for the stated legs' and says 'Stop here until that's addressed.' Turn 3: WebResearcher re-searches, confirms only full lengths exist on Wikipedia, and honestly publishes that it 'could not verify the city-to-city mileage,' but then re-presents the same full-length-based $14.25 as the conditional answer. Turn 4: Finalizer privately acknowledges mileage is 'unverified' but decides '14.25 if we interpret those lengths correctly' is 'enough' and emits FINAL ANSWER: $14.25.
open_ended_diagnosis: The dominant cause is single-agent capability/structural: the actual driving distance for the two legs (which Wikipedia does not tabulate city-to-city) had to be estimated or looked up off-Wikipedia, and no agent ever did so. WebResearcher took the path of least resistance — sum the two full interstate lengths — even though it privately recognized the route was geographically incoherent (Cincinnati is not on I-40). The Critic performed genuinely good critique (it correctly diagnosed the exact bug), so this is NOT a case of the team being blind to the error. The misalignment is in the team's response to that correct critique: the Critic's substantive demand ('verify the actual mileage for the stated legs') was treated as satisfiable by WebResearcher merely restating that it cannot verify the mileage, after which the Finalizer rubber-stamped the unverified number. This is false trust / verification theater layered on a capability gap: the system had a correct internal signal that the answer was wrong but lacked any mechanism (or will) to either compute the real leg distances or refuse to finalize. The deposit-rate side was actually fine (Maine 5 cents, gold consistent with 5 cents); the error is entirely in mileage, hence ~285 bottles vs the gold-implied ~160.
reasoning_vs_published: The richest divergence is WebResearcher Turn 1: its private reasoning openly states 'Cincinnati is on I-75, not I-40, so I need to think about switching highways' and 'The instruction to follow I-40 from Los Angeles to Cincinnati might just be hypothetical' — a real recognition that summing full lengths is not the stated legs. Yet the published message drops all of this doubt and asserts a clean '- Total trip distance: 5,656.35 mi ... So the refund is 285 × $0.05 = $14.25,' presenting a known-shaky figure as supported (info-distortion / unreflective publishing). The Critic, by contrast, published its private doubt faithfully ('The route mileage is not actually demonstrated ... The teammate used the full Wikipedia lengths ... which are not the same thing as the mileage for those city-to-city legs') and even gated progress ('Stop here until that's addressed') — good ToM about what the team needed. That correct, published correction was then effectively ignored (2.5): Turn-3 WebResearcher's reasoning only plans to 'send a concise message to the team regarding my inability to verify the route mileage' — it never attempts the fetch_url of route detail or an off-Wikipedia estimate the Critic asked for, and re-publishes $14.25. The Finalizer's reasoning is the clearest reasoning-action mismatch: 'A critic mentions it's unverified ... we can't confirm details from Wikipedia and only have full lengths available ... I have enough to provide a reasonable answer,' then it emits the very number it just called unverified.
